And presenting the proclamation this evening is Mr. Page. Thank you. The proclamation celebrating Martin Luther King Jr. Day. Whereas just a century after the Emancipation Proclamation in 1963, Dr. King and allied forces marched on Washington and delivered the revered "I Have a Dream" speech, advocating for the end of racial segregation and societal inequalities.

And whereas Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. and other civil rights leaders devoted their lives to the expansion of civil rights and public service to all Americans. And whereas, in honoring his legacy, Martin Luther King Jr. Day is the only federal holiday designated as a national day of service to encourage all Americans to volunteer to improve their communities.

And whereas Altmouth County Public Schools' mission is working together as a team, we will end the predictive value of race, class, gender, and special capacities for our children's success through high-quality teaching and learning for all.

We seek to build relationships with families and communities to ensure that every student succeeds. We will know every student. Albemarle County Public Schools values are centered around equity, excellence, family and community, and wellness, and now therefore be it proclaimed that Albemarle County Public Schools do hereby honor and celebrate January 20, 2025 as Martin Luther King Jr. Day and encourage our employees and residents to work toward his vision for a more equitable and inclusive society. On behalf of the student representatives and Western Albemarle High School, I appreciate the opportunity to speak with you today to share some updates and concerns from the student body.

First, racism and discrimination continues to be a critical issue across all schools with the prevalence of derogatory and hateful remarks becoming increasingly common post-election results. Although the atmosphere slightly varies among schools, it is imperative that we continue to strive towards fostering inclusive and diverse learning environments for students.

In order to uplift cultural diversity, Western Albemarle High School is in the process of planning our second Better Together Cultural Celebration Night in April. The event will intermingle the uniquely distinct identities of various affinity groups, such as YAPIC, the Young Asian American and Pacific Islanders of Charlottesville, Alianza Hispanica, Mocha Wocha, and the Gay Student Alliance through interactive cultural activities, games, food, and music.

Additionally, we are employing initiatives in order to combat discrimination in schools. Students from Western Student Senate Division are collaborating on projects such as Disrupting Hate Initiatives, planning to incorporate anti-racism workshops into potential professional development days for teachers, and advising faculty on how to respond to acts of discrimination in classrooms.

We plan to further collaborate with large student organizations such as WAAS Leadership and WAAS Athletic Department in order to increase student participation and engagement for these causes. At Albemarle High School, similar work is being done to increase cultural awareness and uplift marginalized communities.

Albemarle's chapter of YAPIC is hosting their annual Lunar New Year celebration, preparing foods from various Asian cultures for their student body, both increasing student unity, engagement, and collaboration. We are grateful for the board's continued support as we strive towards creating more equitable, diverse, and inclusive environments for all students.

Thank you. Thank you. Thank you, Margaret. I just want to take a moment to share some information with the Albemarle County School Board. I want to thank you for this opportunity to address an important topic on the minds of many in our community. Recent inquiries about the potential impact of immigration enforcement activities on our schools have prompted timely discussions and preparations within our leadership team and the school board.

And I just want to update you. Above all else, I want to assure our students and their families that our schools are and will remain a safe and welcoming place for all. Outlaw County Public Schools does not, and may not, and will not, ask students or families about their immigration status.

Furthermore, all student education records are private and protected by the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act, commonly known as FERPA. These records will not be shared with any government agency unless presented with a valid warrant or judicial subpoena.

We understand the concern about immigration officials potentially appearing at our schools. Recently, I was asked about the role of our school resource officers. I want to be clear that students or their family members will not be questioned, detained, or taken into custody on ACPS premises except when a law enforcement officer presents a valid warrant or an arrest on criminal charges.

Even in those rare circumstances, and we've had no inquiries to date, I would say that, our protocol requires school-based leaders to notify the school division council who will manage all interactions with law enforcement and presently does that. We recognize that school bus stops are an extension of our schools and play a critical role in providing students with access to education. Following federal policies, guidance, school bus stops, like school campuses, have long been considered sensitive locations.

Immigration enforcement actions at these locations have been strongly discouraged. Recent changes to immigration enforcement policies have eliminated previous guidelines that restricted immigration officers from making arrests at sensitive locations, such as schools and churches.

These changes could potentially allow officers to conduct enforcement activities in these locations. It is still important to note, however, that such actions are all subject to legal protocols, including the need for a warrant in certain circumstances.

FERPA, which protects student educational records, remains in effect and should continue to safeguard private student information, again, unless specific exceptions apply under the law. We will do everything we can to ensure that public schools and associated spaces remain safe and secure for students and families.

We encourage any family concerned about immigration enforcement at or near schools or school bus stops to contact us or trusted community partners. We aim to provide support, information, and resources to ensure all students can safely travel to and from school and attend school in peace.

To further support our schools and families, our Office of Community Engagement has distributed written materials outlining these protocols and resources available to families who feel they may be facing information related challenges.

We're also fortunate to work closely with a network of community partners to ensure families have access to the support they need. While none of us can predict the future, we remain committed to our core values of equity, excellence, community, and well-being.

We stand ready to protect and support all students, staff, and families to the fullest extent of our abilities. Thank you for your continued trust and collaboration as we navigate this together. Thank you. Thank you, Dr. Haas. Is there any other school board or superintendent business?

We are aware that one of the reasons for the program's termination was low participation. However, the assessment fails to take into account that the program was opened right at the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic.

Numerous other educational programs faced enrollment issues, and this one was no different, especially due to the virtual nature caused by the pandemic. Furthermore, the program's participation rate has already doubled this year with the inclusion of freshmen, which is an encouraging sign of growth that should not be overlooked and was only changed somewhat recently.

Additionally, after researching other junior ROTC programs nationwide, we discovered that there is a contractual requirement for a 12-month notice before termination.
